qs.q: Reflex arc components consist of neurons with distinct structural and functional classifications. What is the structural classification of an afferent (sensory) neuron?
qs.e: Afferent (sensory) neurons are structurally unipolar or pseudounipolar. Efferent motor neurons are typically multipolar, while interneurons are often bipolar.

ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: A reflex arc is an automatic neural circuit that mediates a reflex response, linking a sensory stimulus to an effector organ through a spinal or brainstem synapse. It allows rapid, involuntary protection or adjustment without conscious thought.

sections.p: A reflex arc consists of a sensory receptor, afferent neuron, integration centre, efferent neuron, and an effector organ. The pathway is typically short, often confined to the spinal cord, enabling a swift response.

When a stimulus activates a receptor, an action potential travels along the afferent neuron to the integration centre. A synapse relays the signal to an efferent neuron, which then stimulates the effector to produce a response.

t.b: Assesses motor neuron integrity; abnormal activity suggests peripheral neuropathy or spinal cord lesion.
Measures conduction velocity; slowed rates indicate demyelination or axonal loss.
Detects spinal cord pathology; abnormal protein or cells suggest infection or inflammation.

sections.p: The integration centre can be a single interneuron or a network of interneurons. Modulation by descending pathways allows voluntary override or adjustment of reflex magnitude.

t.b: Evaluates integrity of reflex arc; absent or exaggerated responses guide diagnosis.

sections.p: Disruption at any component can blunt or exaggerate reflexes. Common causes include peripheral neuropathy, spinal cord compression, demyelinating disease, or toxic exposure.
b: Spinal cord compression → absent or hyperactive reflexes

t.b: Identifies compressive lesions; abnormal signal suggests demyelination.
Elevated levels confirm lead toxicity; normal levels rule out.

sections.p: Reflex testing is a quick bedside tool to localise neurological lesions, assess autonomic function, and monitor disease progression or treatment response.

t.b: Normal vs. diminished vs. hyperactive; guides differential diagnosis.
Absent indicates optic nerve or brainstem lesion; constriction confirms intact pathway.

sections.p: Remember the mnemonic S-A-I-E-E: Sensory, Afferent, Integration, Efferent, Effector. A classic example is the withdrawal reflex to pain.
b: Withdrawal reflex steps: pain → afferent → spinal cord → interneuron → efferent → muscle contraction

t.a: Clinical scenario: patient with loss of ankle reflex
t.b: Suggests S1 radiculopathy or peripheral neuropathy; further imaging or EMG needed.

faq.q: What is the difference between a reflex and a reflex arc?
faq.a: A reflex is the observable response; the reflex arc is the underlying neural pathway that produces it.

faq.q: Can a reflex be voluntarily suppressed?
faq.a: Yes, descending cortical pathways can inhibit reflexes, allowing voluntary control.

faq.q: Why are some reflexes absent in newborns?
faq.a: Neonatal reflexes mature over weeks; absence may indicate developmental delay or neurological injury.
